lesson: Week 2, Lesson 1: How to prompt any AI model: context, roles and constraints

beats.text: Two people ask Claude for a caption for their cake business. One gets something generic. The other gets a caption she could post as it is.
Same model, same day. The second person just gave it more to work with.
There are no magic words in prompting. You're briefing someone smart who knows nothing about you.
Brief it the way you'd brief a new freelancer on their first day, and Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini all do better. Everything in this lesson works in all three.
The model knows a lot about cakes. It knows nothing about your cakes. Whatever it doesn't know, it fills in with the average, and the average is where generic writing comes from.
So give it the facts only you have. Who the work is for, in one sentence. What you're selling or saying.
What makes you different, with a real detail. And where the work will appear: Instagram, an email, or a WhatsApp status.
Your Claude Project from week one already holds most of this. In a fresh chat anywhere else, paste it in.
A role tells the model which kind of expert to answer as. A copywriter for small Lagos food businesses gives you a different answer from a food blogger.
Keep roles plain and specific. Words like world-class and expert add nothing. The useful part is the job and the audience.
Constraints do most of the work. They answer the question the model would ask you if it could: when is this finished?
Length, like under 50 words or three bullet points. Format, like a table, or plain text you can paste into WhatsApp.
What it must include, such as the price, the deadline and the delivery area. And what it must avoid: words you hate, claims you can't prove, hashtags.
Last week you defined done for an agent. This is the same habit on a smaller job.
Here's Amaka's first attempt: write a caption for my red velvet cake.
Her second sets the role: you write Instagram captions for a home bakery in Lekki, Lagos. Customers are mostly women ordering birthday cakes for family, often at short notice.
Then the facts: an 8 inch red velvet, ₦25,000, same-day delivery in Lekki for orders before 2pm. Customers keep saying it isn't too sweet.
Then the constraints: two options, each under 50 words. Include the price and the 2pm cutoff. No hashtags, and don't use the words indulge or delectable.
The second prompt is longer, and it saves her three rounds of make it shorter and you forgot the price.
When you have one piece of work you like, paste it in and say: match its length and tone, but don't copy its words.
One real example teaches the model more than a paragraph describing what you want. That's why your skill from week one has a section called what good looks like.

chapters.label: When to start a fresh chat

beats.text: Long chats drift. The model gives weight to everything earlier in the conversation, including the three drafts you rejected.
If you've corrected the same thing twice, stop. Open a new chat and write one better brief that includes what you learned.
Your task: write a prompt with context, a role and constraints for a real job you have this week. The next lesson explains why arguing longer doesn't fix a bad answer.
